title: Natural complexity arises because natural systems behave like typical programs

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Natural complexity arises because natural systems behave like typical programs

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The great complexity seen across physical, biological and other natural systems is explained by those systems operating like typical simple programs, which commonly produce complex behavior, rather than by any special or supernatural source of complexity.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: For all it takes is that systems in nature operate like typical programs and then it follows that their behavior will often be complex.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 1, “The Foundations for a New Kind of Science”; section “An Outline of Basic Ideas” (from p. 1), p. 3. Scope: complex-looking physical, biological and other natural systems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch01-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.22

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Restricted case studies are possible, but existing observations do not identify whether nature operates like typical programs. The broad explanatory and exclusionary wording has weak discrimination from many rival mechanisms.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For selected natural phenomena, fit specified simple-program generative models and rival mechanistic models to observations, then compare predictive likelihood and complexity. Better program-model predictions would support a restricted version, while systematic failure would refute it in those domains.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Similar-looking output does not identify a natural generative mechanism.

The claim spans nearly all natural complexity.

Typical program and natural complexity are undefined without substantial choices.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.25
data existence: 0.35
data adequacy: 0.12
discriminating power: 0.15
analysis feasibility: 0.2

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing morphology and developmental-genetics collections cover a few well-studied organisms and support case-by-case comparisons. They do not contain the generative rules of physical, biological, and other natural systems at the scope the claim states. A program that draws a similar picture is compatible with rival explanations, so current data can probe examples and cannot settle the general causal claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For a sample of physical and biological systems, identify the actual local rules and compare their complexity and typicality with simple programs, then ask whether those rules account for the observed complexity better than selection or continuum equations. A visual match between a program and a natural pattern would not confirm the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The rules of most natural systems have not been measured at the relevant grain.

Resemblance of output does not identify the mechanism that produced it.

Selection, reaction-diffusion, and continuum models can generate the same complexity.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.4

data existence: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.4
